The best hair oils for frizz, hydration and shine, according to experts

Hair oils 101

Charlotte Brundrett
@charbrundrett
11 min read
October 9, 2026 - 8:00AM

  • Understanding hair oils

  • Essential oils v carrier oils

Looking for the best hair oil for your haircare routine? We compare top-rated oils including rosemary, argan, castor and more to help you choose the right one for your hair type and concerns.

From combating stubborn frizz to restoring high-gloss shine, adding a top-rated hair oil is one of the fastest ways to revive dry, damaged strands.

However, not all hair oils are created equal, and using the wrong formula for your hair type can leave your scalp feeling greasy rather than nourished.

While the right formula can help reduce frizz, tame flyaways, soften dry strands and promote shine, different hair types require different ingredients.

To separate viral trends from proven results, we consulted top hair experts Chelcey Salinger, principal trichologist and executive director at the International Association of Trichologists, and trichologist Jane Davies, founder of The Hair Physio.

Here is their definitive guide on how to choose — and use — the best hair oil for your routine.

Hair oils: At a glance

  • Hair oiling v hair growth: Hair oiling conditions the hair shaft, adds shine and prevents snap breakage, making hair look fuller, but it does not stimulate new growth from the follicles.
  • Penetrating v coating oils: Penetrating oils (coconut, argan, avocado) sink deep into damaged strands to hydrate from within. Coating oils (jojoba, castor, macadamia) sit on the surface to lock out humidity, tame frizz, and add external gloss.
  • Carrier v essential oils: Never apply pure essential oils (such as rosemary or peppermint) directly to the scalp without a carrier base (like jojoba or sweet almond) as they can trigger severe rashes and scalp irritation.
  • Hair porosity matters: If your hair feels greasy or weighed down after oiling, you likely have low-porosity hair using a heavy coating oil. Swap to a lightweight, penetrating formula instead.

What is hair oiling and how does it work?

Hair oiling is a traditional hair care practice that involves massaging a plant-based oil directly into the scalp and working it through the lengths and ends of the hair.

The ancient technique has gained global popularity as an essential routine for boosting hair health, nourishing strands, improving shine and reducing frizz.

Jane says the practice can be beneficial for hair, provided expectations are realistic.

“Oils make our hair feel softer, smoother and more manageable while improving shine and reducing friction and breakage,” she says.

“These cosmetic improvements can make the hair appear healthier and fuller, but they are not the same as stimulating new growth from the follicles.”

Benefits of hair oils

While viral social media trends often tout oils as a miracle fix for thinning and hair growth, trichologists emphasise that their primary benefits are cosmetic rather than cellular.

“I really like oils as conditioning agents for the hair shaft,” Chelcey says.

“They can reduce friction, improve softness and manageability, and help dry or damaged hair look and feel healthier.

“But conditioning the hair shaft and stimulating hair growth are two very different things.”

Understanding hair oils: penetrating v coating oil

Depending on the molecular size of the product, hair oils tend to fall into two categories, each serving very different purposes.

Coating oils

Oils with larger molecules cannot penetrate the hair shaft, so they sit on the outside of the cuticle instead.

  • Used for: External protection
  • Best coating oils: Castor oil, jojoba oil, macadamia oil and grapeseed oil
  • Best for: Hair types prone to frizz, or for people living in humid conditions
  • How they work: These oils serve as a protective barrier against the elements, much like paw paw ointment does for chapped lips. They are excellent smoothing agents that lock out moisture and add external shine.

Penetrating oils

For an oil to actually penetrate the scalp and hair shaft, it needs to have a small molecular structure.

  • Used for: Internal hydration
  • Best penetrating oils: Coconut oil, avocado oil, olive oil and argan oil
  • Best for: Dry, damaged or highly porous hair that needs deep hydration and structural repair, as well as low porosity hair that requires lightweight oils to avoid product build-up
  • How they work: Because of their small molecules, these oils help moisturise and improve the condition of dry or damaged hair. Oils rich in lauric acid and protein fall into this category and are excellent for strengthening the hair.

Why hair porosity matters

Your hair’s porosity – how easily it absorbs and retains moisture – will dictate which oil you should use.

People with low porosity hair have smooth, tightly closed cuticles. This makes the hair prone to product build-up, which can make it stiff and ultimately contribute to breakage.

Because low porosity hair is notoriously difficult to penetrate, many people with this hair type avoid oils altogether, complaining that it leaves their hair feeling heavy, flat or greasy.

However, that “heavy” feeling is simply the result of using a coating oil that sits on top of the hair rather than sinks into it.

If you have low porosity hair, it’s best to swap to a lightweight, penetrating oil instead.

Essential oils v carrier oils: What’s the difference?

Another area that confuses beginners is the distinction between essential oils and carrier oils in haircare.

Essential oils

Essential oils are highly potent, concentrated plant extracts.

In the context of hair oiling, they are primarily used to treat the scalp rather than the lengths of the hair, but further research is needed to prove the haircare benefits of these oils.

  • Popular options: Peppermint oil, lavender oil, rosemary oil
  • Benefits: Some essential oils are being investigated for their potential scalp and hair benefits, although further research is needed.

Because they are so highly concentrated, essential oils can easily trigger skin rashes and allergic reactions.

Chelcey recommends readers consider their own skin concerns before diving into scalp treatments.

“I’m generally cautious about applying oils directly to the scalp,” she says.

“The scalp is skin, and many oils are occlusive and can be problematic for people who are prone to an oily scalp, folliculitis, dandruff or seborrhoeic dermatitis.”

She adds a crucial reminder for anyone influenced by TikTok trends: “Something being ‘natural’ or beneficial for the hair shaft doesn’t automatically mean it’s beneficial for the scalp.”

Use products only as directed, and see your doctor if you experience any symptoms.

Carrier oils

Because essential oils are highly concentrated plant extracts, they can cause severe scalp irritation if applied directly to the skin. This is where carrier oils come in.

As the name suggests, these base oils are used to carry potent essential oils safely to your scalp and hair, acting as a soothing buffer.

Extracted from nuts, seeds or kernels, carrier oils are packed with fatty acids, vitamins and antioxidants.

If you are creating a DIY hair oil blend at home, a carrier oil will make up the vast majority of the mixture, with only a few drops of your chosen essential oil added for targeted potency.

  • Popular options: Jojoba oil, sweet almond oil, grapeseed oil
  • Benefits: Carrier oils are used to dilute essential oils so they are safe for topical application. Mild and gentle, these base oils are packed with fatty acids, making them a solid option for locking in hydration and nourishing dry, damaged hair.

The best hair oils for hair growth

#1. Rosemary oil

Among the most common essential oils in haircare, rosemary oil is a clear standout.

Rosemary oil has attracted research interest in its potential effects on the scalp, although evidence for its effectiveness in promoting hair growth remains limited.

#2. Pumpkin seed oil

What makes pumpkin seed oil (PSO) unique among hair oils is that it contains phytosterols and fatty acids, which have the ability to inhibit 5-alpha reductase (the enzyme that changes testosterone into hair-thinning dihydrotestosterone, or DHT).

However, this does not establish a hair-growth benefit. More research and clinical trials are needed to back claims that topical PSO can stimulate hair growth.

#3. Castor oil

Castor oil has long been heralded for its multi-use properties, including its hair benefits.

While there’s little evidence to support castor oil directly contributing to hair growth, consistent use has been shown to have a moisturising effect, which may help reduce breakage and, indirectly, contribute to longer hair.

The best hair oils for hydration, frizz and shine

#1. Argan oil

One of the most commercially popular hair oils on the market, argan oil gained prominence due to its hydrating properties, which include vitamin E and essential fatty acids.

The oil can also function as a pre-treatment to reduce damage from hair dyes and UV exposure.

#2. Coconut oil

According to Jane, coconut oil is one of the best studied natural oils. “Its structure allows it to penetrate the hair fibre,” she says.

Because it contains lauric acid, the oil can also help protect the hair shaft from protein loss. 

“This may improve length retention by reducing breakage, but it does not stimulate new follicular growth.”

#3. Jojoba oil

A common beauty staple, jojoba oil is equally popular as a face and hair oil. When it comes to its hair benefits, jojoba stands out as a leave-in conditioner for dry or brittle hair types due to its emollient properties, which have the added benefit of improving hair fiber breakage resistance.

How to apply hair oil correctly

There’s no real streamlined technique for applying hair oil.

Ultimately, it comes down to whether you’re applying the oil as a pre-shampoo treatment or a hair oiling treatment that you plan to wash off, or as a finishing product after you’ve washed your hair.

In the latter case, it’s best to detangle the hair first and then apply a small, pea-sized amount of oil as you don’t want to weigh down your hair with excess product.

If your hair absorbs the product quickly, add more – little by little – until your hair feels smooth and soft to touch.

For hair oil treatments, it doesn’t matter too much if you’re a bit heavy-handed, as you’ll be washing out the product.

That said, you don’t want to start with too much oil either as you’ll be focusing on massaging your scalp and running it through the ends of your hair with your fingers.

Hair oil v shampoo

When it comes to haircare routines, it’s easy to overdo it with products, but incorporating hair oil doesn’t have to be complicated.

The first thing to consider is what hair concern you want to target.

If you want a product that can serve as a smoothing, anti-frizz agent, then seek out hair oil that can function as a finishing product at the end of your washing and styling routine.

On the flipside, if you’re looking to moisturise a dry-feeling scalp, choose a product that is specifically formulated for scalp application.

This kind of oil tends to be heavier on the hair, which is why it functions best as a pre-shampoo treatment that can be washed out.

 

Hair oil FAQs

Everything you need to know about hair oiling, scalp health and choosing the right products for your routine.

Do hair oils work directly on the scalp?

Yes, provided it’s a scalp-friendly hair oil. Always look at the product’s packaging which should clearly state whether it’s intended for scalp application or not. The issue with applying a hair oil not intended for use on the scalp is that it can actually cause irritation.

Can hair oils be misused?

Yes. Due to the varying types of hair oils and their specific uses and benefits, certain oils aren’t intended for scalp or hair length application.

“Hair oils can definitely be misused, particularly when it comes to scalp oils that people purchase online without professional advice or guidance,” Scissor & Stone salon head stylist Aimee Green says.

“For example, many people who think they have dandruff actually have a dry or dehydrated scalp, and the two require very different approaches.

“Dandruff can also be hereditary, so it’s important to understand what your scalp actually needs before introducing an oil.”

If you’re unsure about the root cause of your hair concern, Aimee encourages readers to

speak with a professional to identify the right product and understand how much to use and how often, rather than assuming what will work best for your hair.

Do hair oils actually work for hair growth?

While hair oils are generally safe for topical use, the science behind whether they can actively stimulate new growth is complex.

According to Chelcey Salinger, principal trichologist and executive director of the International Association of Trichologists, new research suggests human hair follicles are able to express olfactory or “smell” receptors that can be activated by fragrance molecules, which could be promising for future hair growth products.

That said, Chelcey cautions readers against assuming everyday hair oiling is a miracle cure.

“It’s a fascinating area of research, but it’s important not to extrapolate findings like these to scalp oiling in general,” Chelcey says.

 “(The findings) show us that certain specific molecules can interact with the biology of the hair follicle – not that applying any essential or carrier oil to the scalp will stimulate hair growth.”

Should I apply hair oil to wet or dry hair?

It depends on the type of hair oil and whether it penetrates the hair shaft or not.

If it doesn’t, it’s most likely to sit on the outer layer of hair and make it appear flat and oily.

Can hair oil cause build-up if left on too long?

Yes, especially if it’s not lightweight and sits on the cuticle.

Win $3k cash: Take our women’s health survey

If you tend to use hair oils regularly, it’s important to use a clarifying shampoo or scalp exfoliant every few washes to reduce product build-up.

How often should I oil my hair?

It really comes down to personal preference and the condition and type of your hair.

Is hair oil actually good for hair?

Yes, hair oil has a range of benefits when it comes to moisturising the hair and protecting it against heat damage.

While there is some research to back some of the purported benefits of rosemary oil, further research is needed to support the efficacy of other hair oils.

Can I leave in hair oil overnight?

While leaving in hair oil overnight can benefit those with thick, coarse hair, it should still done sparingly.  

Do you have to wash out hair oil?

Not always. Washing out hair oil is only necessary for pre-shampoo treatments, overnight treatments and hair oiling.

If you’re using a small amount of oil as a finishing or smoothing agent, it serves the same purpose as a leave-in conditioner.

Are there any oils you should never use on hair?

Yes. Anything with petroleum or mineral oil is not recommended for use on the hair, because these oils sit on the hair’s surface and coat the follicles in a film that can block moisture from entering the hair shaft (in addition to being notoriously difficult to wash out).

Most cooking oils are ruled out for a similar reason, especially olive oil – contrary to popular belief – because it’s moderately comedogenic, making it unsuitable for use on the scalp.
